newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Economists say Israeli budget cuts on target.
newsitem.headline: Economists say Israeli budget cuts on target.

text.p: The Israeli Treasury's latest round of budget cuts should keep next year's deficit on target even if further compromises are made to win parliament's approval, economists and market analysts said on Tuesday.
"If they lower spending by 6.7 billion shekels or so, this will certainly give them the 2.8 percent of gross domestic product," said a bank economist, referring to the Treasury's 1997 deficit goal.
On Monday, the cabinet approved a further 1.2 billion shekels in spending cuts on top of the 4.9 billion shekels contained in the original budget package.
In addition, the cabinet voted 600 million shekels in new non-tax revenues from such sources as the sale of homes in West Bank settlements and higher motor vehicle violation fines.
"The general strategy is correct - no new taxes, no reductions in infrastructure spending," said Yoram Gabbay, chairman of Peilim fund managers and a former Treasury budget director.
But, he warned, opposition in parliament will coalesce once the details of the new spending cuts are revealed at the end of the week.
Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, said he believed that the government had already fudged on its pledge of no new taxes.
"So far direct taxes haven't been raised -- but increased traffic fines is a tax by another name," he said.
He and other analysts said it was likely the Treasury would have to accept direct tax increases as well to win parliament's approval.

The key question will then be whether the final budget package wins the favour of the Bank of Israel. The business community and financial markets are counting on the budget cuts to set off a chain of developments they hope will lift the sagging Israeli economy.
A sizable budget cut will help convince the Bank of Israel to lower real interest rates.

That should ease the upward pressure on the Israeli shekel, which most analysts say is overvalued and has hurt Israel's export-driven economy. A rise in exports would also help narrow Israel's current account deficit.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel expressed concerns about the size and composition of Monday's spending cuts, but analysts said they still expect the bank to cut rates.
"Don't expect Frenkel to say he's satisfied with everything," said Gidi Halpern, investments manager at Meitav Securities and Investments. "It's enough that he supports the direction."
He said the market was anticipating a lowering of the short-term base rate -- now 15.2 percent -- by up to 1.5 percentage points over the next two to three months.
But the bank economist warned: "I'm not sure all the conditions will be met."
He said a small to medium rate cut, for instance, would not bring about a depreciation in the shekel.
